source.title: Quantum-enhanced Large Language Models on Quantum Hardware via Cayley Unitary Adapters
source.authors: Borja Aizpurua; Sukhbinder Singh; Augustine Kshetrimayum; S. S. Jahromi; Román Orús

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. but does not test or rely on the stated scaling laws. Its perplexity sweeps vary the size of trained adapters on a fixed compressed model; they do not test power-law fits, extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports WikiText perplexity across Cayley-adapter block sizes and adapter parameter counts, plus perplexity comparisons among Llama adapter configurations. These are adapter-capacity results, not tests of the claim's pretraining scaling laws. The paper also reports downstream benchmarks, but not downstream performance predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. only to motivate memory costs of scale. Its sweeps vary trainable adapter block size on a fixed compressed SmolLM2 backbone and report WikiText perplexity. They involve no pretraining-scale variation in parameters, tokens or compute, no power-law fit, no extrapolation and no compute-optimal analysis. Downstream benchmarks are not related to scale or pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that Cayley unitary adapters, trained classically and run on IBM QPU (2-qubit blocks), improve Llama 3.1 8B WikiText perplexity by 1.43% with about 6K parameters. On compressed SmolLM2, perplexity improves monotonically with block dimension, and the adapters recover 83% of the LAMBADA compression gap. A noise phase transition at 2–3 qubits limits current hardware. They make no claims about pretraining scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: No scaling-law measurement recipe is used; the paper trains adapters on fixed backbones and evaluates their perplexity.
record.method_sensitivity: Adapter block dimension and adapter regime change the reported perplexity; the paper also notes that layer choice matters for adapter outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: On a compressed SmolLM2 backbone (94.8M), 210-layer adapter WikiText PPL falls monotonically as block dimension and adapter parameters grow. For example, the unconstrained regime goes from 34.23 at 505K to 27.01 at 220.2M parameters. No power-law fit is reported, and gains flatten at the largest sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adapter capacity on a frozen compressed backbone reduces perplexity monotonically, but no scaling form is established.

record.code_released: Code is available upon reasonable request.
record.problems: The adapter sweep varies trainable adapter capacity on a fixed compressed backbone rather than scaling pretrained language-model parameters, tokens, or compute. No scaling-law fits, exponents, or extrapolation tests are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Not included: Llama adapter-configuration perplexity comparisons and simulated hardware-noise sweep; these concern adapter configuration and hardware noise rather than tests of the stated scaling laws. Downstream benchmark outcomes are also omitted because they do not measure predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

untested.parts: Loss power law in pretraining parameters, tokens or compute: not tested. Only adapter capacity is varied, on a frozen backbone.
Extrapolation from small to large runs: not tested.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count: not tested.
Power laws in other modalities or regimes: not tested. The adapter-size perplexity trend is not fitted as a power law.
Downstream predictability from scale or loss: not tested.
Fit-dependence of exponents or allocation: not tested.

record.verdict_notes: All rows rightly link to none. They measure post-hoc adapter capacity on a frozen, compressed model, not pretraining loss versus model, data or compute scale. Kaplan et al. is cited only in the introduction.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law behavior of held-out pretraining loss with model parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Whether power-law forms hold in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling-law fits or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.
